email.scenario: You are a volunteer archivist cataloging a historical society's newly donated collection of oral history recordings. While cross-checking the audio files against the donor's intake list, you discover that several recordings are labeled with the wrong interviewee names. The heritage exhibit featuring these recordings opens next month, so the mistake needs to be corrected soon.
email.subject: Mislabeled Names in Oral History Recordings
bullets: Describe the mislabeling problem you found in the recordings.
Explain how you discovered the name mismatches.
Ask the coordinator to confirm once the labels have been corrected.

academicDiscussion.professorPost: This week we're examining a policy some universities have adopted: requiring first-year students to complete a supervised study skills course before they can enroll in upper-level electives. Supporters say it gives students essential tools before they face harder coursework, while critics worry it limits students' freedom to design their own academic path. What do you think? Should universities require this course, or should students be free to choose their own schedule? Why or why not?

studentPosts.name: Priya
studentPosts.post: I think the requirement makes sense. A lot of first-year students, myself included, struggled with time management and note-taking skills that high school never really taught. Building those skills early would have saved me from a rough first semester before I could even think about tackling advanced electives.

studentPosts.name: Marcus
studentPosts.post: I get where Priya's coming from, but I don't think a mandatory course is the right fix. Students come in with very different backgrounds, and forcing everyone through the same class wastes time for those who already have solid study habits. Universities should offer the course as an optional resource instead of requiring it for everyone.
